extracted.intended_audience: high-school mathematical olympiad participants, coaches, and problem-solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, heuristics, and problem-solving standards for tackling high-school level olympiad problems (number theory, combinatorics, geometry, inequalities, sequences). Emphasizes common methods, bounding/attainability, linearization, counting arguments, and choice of analytic vs synthetic approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step approach for extremal (max/min) problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution of such a kind of problems usually involves two steps: First, get an upper bound or a lower bound of the problem using given conditions and well-known inequalities. Secondly, show that such an upper bound or lower bound is attainable, and then is the maximum or minimum value we are looking for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known inequalities to derive an attainable bound, then construct or demonstrate an example attaining that bound. (This remark is given after the first three problems which concern finding maxima/minima.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearize nonlinear sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When we encounter a problem involving a nonlinear sequence, the first thing to do is to linearize and to simplify the problem. Specifically, if it has an expression with radical terms, try to eliminate these terms to get a linear recursive expression of order 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate radicals or nonlinearities to find a second-order linear recurrence; then standard techniques (characteristic polynomials, induction) can be applied. (Used in the solution showing terms are integers and divisibility by 2K.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Count distinct k-term blocks to bound binary sequence length
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that there are at the most 2^k different sections of successive k terms (consisting of 0 and 1). According to this, one can deduce an upper bound on the length of a binary sequence with the property that every two length-k windows are different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For k=5, there are at most 32 different 5-term blocks, implying a maximum sequence length ≤ 32 + (k-1) = 36. This uses the counting / De Bruijn-type argument; one may also try to construct a sequence achieving the bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use divisibility periodicity/counting in consecutive integers
rubrics_metrics.description: Key to some divisibility/minimality problems is finding how many integers divisible by a given d appear among a block of consecutive (odd) numbers; exploit periodicity to derive inequalities on block lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., to determine the least u such that among any u consecutive odd numbers the count of multiples of d is at least that in 1,3,...,2n-1, show counts for specific d (like 2n-1) in certain-length blocks are zero or positive and deduce bounds on u.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-union counting for divisor/coprime problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Denote A as divisors of n and B as integers in [1,n] coprime to n; since intersection A ∩ B contains only 1, one gets d(n) + p(n) = |A| + |B| = |A ∪ B| + 1 < n+1, so d(n)+p(n) ≤ n+1 and often forces small additive constants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count elements in A, B, and their intersection to deduce possible values of c in d(n)+p(n)=n+c; restrict possibilities (here c∈{0,1}) and check small n by direct search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of evaluation (labeling) and transformation for parity problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Parity of counts of adjacent differently-colored pairs can be determined by labeling colors (e.g. red=1, blue=-1), taking products on edges, and/or applying local transformations (flipping a cell's color) and tracking parity changes. The parity is invariant under transformations that change an even number of adjacent-difference counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solution I: label cells with ±1, take product of labels on each adjacent pair; global product yields parity. Solution II: apply color-flipping transformations and track how S (number of good couples) changes (parity flips only when flipping a border cell). Use these invariances to reduce to simpler configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose analytic coordinates vs pure synthetic geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: When geometry is asymmetric or coordinate computations simplify algebraic distances/relations, use analytic (coordinate) methods; otherwise a pure geometric approach (projections, proportional segments) may give a more conceptual proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove a condition involving sums of perpendicular distances or equalities involving projections, set up coordinates to compute expressions explicitly; alternatively construct projections of special centers and use similarity/proportionality for a synthetic proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove one-variable inequalities and sum them
rubrics_metrics.description: For inequalities of the form sum_i f(x_i) ≥ constant, it is natural to prove an inequality for each variable separately (e.g. 4x^3+1>3x for x in [-1,∞)) and then add them to obtain the desired result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove per-variable lower/upper bounds valid for the variable domain, then sum. This was used to find the optimal K in 4(a^3)+1>3a leading to K = 1/4 type arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction combined with modular congruences for divisibility in sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a fixed prime (or integer) divides certain expressions in a recursively defined sequence, use induction on indices and reduce recurrence differences modulo that prime; show base cases then derive next index via congruence relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for a Fibonacci-like sequence with a=3,b=5, prove 5 divides a_k - 2n·3^k by checking small n and using induction from k and k+1 to k+2 via modular arithmetic mod 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremal/graph/Ramsey-style reasoning to bound combinatorial configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: To bound the maximum size of a set under local acquaintance/non-acquaintance constraints, consider degrees, apply Ramsey-type theorems or extremal arguments: show high or low degree leads to forbidden substructures, derive contradictions for large n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., to show at most 8 students can satisfy: 'every three contain two mutual acquaintances' and 'every four contain two non-acquaintances', argue that any vertex with degree ≥6 or ≤n-5 leads to a forbidden 3- or 4-subset, use Ramsey theory to bound n.
